prize_parts.citation: for establishing modern political economics, the formal and empirical analysis of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged, but my confidence is lower than in round 1. B016 is a research programme in which formal theory generates sharp implications about how electoral rules, constitutional design, accountability and state capacity map into taxation, spending and public-goods provision, and in which those implications are then taken to cross-country and within-country data. It made political institutions an object of economic analysis rather than a given. It is about thirty years old, so extension, replication and critique are already in the record. It is a standard part of graduate teaching in public economics, development and political economy. On the common criteria, I weigh contribution, attribution and maturity. The trio of Persson, Tabellini and Besley is, in my judgement, the cleanest cut of the programme. Round 1 gave me no argument that this cut is wrong. It also did not show that B016 beats the strongest rivals on every criterion. The citation should rest on the framework and the programme it generated, not on any single estimated coefficient, and it should be worded around rules and fiscal policy so that it is distinct from the 2024 institutions prize.
statement.case_against: I now weigh three reservations more heavily than before. First, identification is weaker than for the best design-based candidates. Constitutions and electoral systems are not randomly assigned, and Fredriksson and Teorell are right that the cross-country results are in key respects correlational. Later within-country designs help, but they do not erase the problem. Second, the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity leaves a real risk that B016 reads as less novel at the margin. I think the subject matter is distinct, but I cannot rule out a committee judging otherwise. Third, credit between the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands is not cleanly separable, and adjacent contributors (Alesina, deceased; Dixit) fall outside the three-name set. Last, round 1 showed that B001 and B020 each have a case that is at least as strong on one criterion: B001 on attribution, B020 on empirical footprint. Three of the first-place preferences for B016 come from members whose fields are close to mine, and the chair summary is right that these are not three independent assessments.

responses.point: Krusell keeps B016 first with moderate confidence, calls B001 the closest rival and the safer choice if the committee wants cleaner attribution, and says our agreement should not be counted as independent evidence.
responses.response: I agree on both points. Our agreement should carry no evidential weight, and I have tried not to cite it in my own reasoning. I also accept his ranking of B001 as the closest rival. Where I would add to his framing is that B001 is safer on attribution but not clearly stronger on tested content, since several members rightly stress that the protection-for-sale predictions have mixed empirical support. So the choice between B016 and B001 is a trade-off between breadth and clean credit, with no dominant option. I hold B016 first for that reason, narrowly.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He argues that its models make sharper, testable predictions than the constitutional comparisons in B016, whose strongest results remain correlational in key respects, and that B001 has the cleaner two-person attribution.
responses.response: The identification point is fair and I concede it. For constitutional and electoral-rule effects, the empirical side is weaker than the theory. My reply is limited. Sharper predictions in B001 have not produced consistent confirmation, as you and others acknowledge, so testability on paper is not the same as tested content. I also read B016 as having opened a wider programme that public economics, development and political economy continue to use. If the committee weights clean two-person credit and sharpness of the model above breadth, your ordering is defensible and I could accept B001 as the single-part award.

responses.point: Andersson keeps B016 behind B001 for three reasons: apportioning credit across three names, contested identification in constitutional comparisons, and thematic adjacency to the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: Of those three, the apportionment problem and the identification problem are the ones I find most serious, and I have raised both myself. The 2024 overlap I still see as a difference in subject. The 2024 work is about the long-run historical origins of institutional quality, while B016 is about how specific contemporary rules and state capacity map into fiscal policy. That is not a rebuttal of your concern. The committee has to judge whether a citation worded around rules and fiscal outcomes separates the two enough, and I do not think the question is settled. It is the main reason I rank B016 narrowly and not clearly.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first. He treats Melitz as the clear core with Helpman as the natural partner and says the empirical reorientation toward firm-level data is a large scientific change. He holds his view on the missing Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum credit with moderate confidence.
responses.response: In my opening I did not rank B020, and I said I wanted the discussion to test it. After reading the exchange I take it more seriously, and I now name it as an alternative in place of B031. The measurable change in data use, estimation and quantitative policy evaluation is the strongest empirical case on the shortlist. I still see two open points. The credit gap is real under a three-name cap, and I cannot judge whether it is disqualifying without a view on how close the omitted empirical pioneers are to the core. And as I said before, the absence of a trade prize since 2008 is a balance consideration, not merit, so I give it no weight. Your co-authorship disclosure with me is noted, and it is a reason for me to give your view no special weight.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first and B001 below it because the selection and reallocation mechanisms have been checked against firm-level data in many countries, whereas protection-for-sale has not been confirmed as consistently. He also says that stacking both Helpman strands in one award would be wrong.
responses.response: I agree that the Committee should choose one Helpman strand and should not stack them, and that Helpman's presence in both should not make either route easier. On the substance, your empirical-confirmation argument is the strongest one against B001 and I weigh it. It is also, on the same logic, a point I must apply to my own candidate: B016's empirical confirmation is weaker than B020's. That is why B020 is now an alternative for me. I do not think it settles the ranking, because the criteria also include breadth of the research programme and cleanness of credit, where B020 has a gap. My co-authorship with you on a 2026 paper is noted and is not a connection to any candidate.

uncertainties: Whether a citation limited to electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity in fiscal policy separates B016 from the 2024 institutions prize enough to resolve the overlap concern.
Whether the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands can be defended as one three-name achievement when their credit is not cleanly separable.
How much weight the committee should place on a programme with weaker identification than design-based work, compared with a clean two-person framework (B001) or a wider empirical footprint (B020).

Whether the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum omission is disqualifying for B020, which bears on whether it is a stronger second choice than B001. I have not independently verified the finer attribution.
My assessments rest on my recollection of the literature and on colleagues' written positions. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or any candidate's affiliations.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal is established by my supplied profile, which lists no co-authorship with Persson, Tabellini, Besley or any other credited candidate. I update my round-1 note in two ways. First, several members have flagged possible Swedish-institutional proximity of some B016 candidates to the Committee. I am a professor at IIES, Stockholm University. As far as I recall, Torsten Persson has long been associated with IIES. This is not documented in my supplied profile and I have not verified it, so I disclose it and do not adjudicate it. Second, my own research on dynamic political economy (the welfare state, the dynamics of government, with Storesletten, Rodríguez Mora, Zilibotti and Krusell) is thematically adjacent to B016. As chair I preferred B016 in round 1, and the chair summary records that. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Krusell, Boppart and Friberg, none of whom is a candidate, and Krusell and I agree on B016 without that agreement being independent evidence. I name B001 and B020 as alternatives and would accept either as a single-part award if the committee prefers it.
